entities.name: Harmala
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Harmala ibn Kahil, an archer in the Umayyad army, is primarily remembered in Islamic history for his direct role in the tragedy of Karbala on 10 Muharram, 61 AH (October 10, 680 CE). Serving under the command of figures loyal to Yazid I, Harmala's actions contributed significantly to the brutal suppression of Husayn ibn Ali's small contingent. His historical footprint is inextricably linked to one of the most pivotal and emotionally charged events in the early Islamic period, an event that profoundly deepened the schism between Sunni and Shia Islam and continues to resonate in religious observance and identity. He represents a specific, chilling aspect of the Umayyad military's ruthlessness in consolidating power.

The core event defining Harmala's legacy occurred during the final hours of the Battle of Karbala. As Husayn ibn Ali's camp was surrounded and his companions systematically killed, Husayn emerged, pleading for water for his infant son, Ali al-Asghar. Harmala, positioned among the Umayyad forces, reportedly fired an arrow that struck the infant's throat, killing him instantly. This act, described in numerous historical and religious accounts, became a particularly poignant detail in the narrative of Husayn's martyrdom, symbolizing the extreme cruelty inflicted upon the Prophet Muhammad's family and the Umayyad regime's complete disregard for sacred lineage.

The killing of Ali al-Asghar by Harmala ibn Kahil left an indelible mark on the collective memory of Shia Muslims, transforming the infant into a powerful symbol of innocence and suffering. This act, among others at Karbala, solidified the Umayyad Caliphate's image as tyrannical and illegitimate in Shia tradition, fueling centuries of religious and political resistance. Harmala himself became a figure of infamy, his name invoked in Ashura commemorations as an embodiment of the forces opposing justice and piety, reinforcing the foundational narratives of Shia identity and martyrdom.
